audit.reasoning: Quote check: every fragment of the deciding quotation is present at the stated thesis pages in the held scanned of Hesse 1993 (page-image grade appropriate: scan without text). Deciding source is the only dedicated phonology of Imyan Tehit (M.A. thesis, fieldwork-based); Glottolog's two phonology entries are this thesis and its 1995 journal revision, which I downloaded from the LLM archive and which repeats the stress analysis verbatim. Hesse 2000 (NUSA 47, downloaded) restates the rule as: one stress per non-compound word, usually penult but ultimate not uncommon, and a syllable with complex onset/nucleus/coda 'always carries the word stress'; schwa syllables never stressed. This matches the catalog's weight-hedged/weight-sensitive (tentative) coding (default penult-of-root, branching-constituent attraction, weight class onset-or-other, pervasive lexical residue, no secondary stress). sources.citation: Hesse, Ronald G. 1995. Syllable structure in Imyan Tehit. Language and Linguistics in Melanesia 26(2): 101-171. [revised version of the 1993 thesis]
sources.quote: Same analysis as the thesis, verbatim in the key passages: default = penult of root (marking convention), branching onset/nucleus/word-final yC coda attracts word stress; adds explicitly that non-compound words carry a single stress and epenthetic schwa is never stressed and only pretonic.
sources.locator: p.112 (sec. 2.4.2): '[j] followed by /t s n/. The vowel preceding them is always stressed'; p.119: 'Evidently, word stress is attracted to any syllable having a branching subsyllabic structure, whether onset, coda, or nucleus.. not the presence of a prevocalic glide alone.. but rather a true branching structure'; p.120 (30) 'Word-Initial Onset Glide Always Indicates Stress'; p.131: schwa 'is never stressed.. restricted to pretonic position.. non-compound words in Tehit carry only one stressed syllable'; p.144 (App. 1): stress written 'only if it does not fall on the penultimate syllable of the root morpheme'.
sources.note: Published, revised version of the deciding 1993 thesis; citable journal locus for the same stress statements (pp. 112, 119-120, 131, 144).

sources.citation: Hesse, Ronald. 2000. Tehit. In Ger P. Reesink (ed.), Studies in Irian Languages, Part II (NUSA 47), 25-33. Jakarta: Universitas Katolik Indonesia Atma Jaya.
sources.quote: 'All Tehit words have lexical stress. Stress in polysyllabic non-compound words is relegated to a single syllable, usually the penultimate, but word-ultimate stress is not uncommon. If a word contains a syllable having complex structure, whether due to a complex onset, nucleus or coda, then that syllable always carries the word stress. Degenerate syllables never carry stress and are restricted to pretonic position.'
sources.note: Author's own one-paragraph stress rule (p.25): single stress, usually penult, ultimate 'not uncommon', complex syllable 'always carries the word stress' -- the cleanest quotable statement of the exceptionless weight clause plus lexical residue; supports exceptions='pervasive' and the weight-sensitive (tentative) classification.

sources.citation: Flassy, Don A. L. and W. A. L. Stokhof. 1979. A note on Tehit (Bird's Head - Irian Jaya). NUSA 7: 35-83.
sources.quote: 'The place of the stress is distinctive:' with pairs /wqoÍT/ 'wood' vs /UqoÍT/ 'he pushes', /wási/ 'he is floating away' vs /wasí/ 'he has a look at', /wáasi/ 'it/he is suitable' vs /waasí/ 'not at all, without' (stress marked with a vertical tick throughout the phoneme-contrast lists; p.79 orthography note 'Stress is not indicated'). Different (Flassy's) dialect basis; several pairs are prefixed-vs-monomorphemic, consistent with Hesse's root-based count.
sources.note: Independent (native-speaker) source stating stress placement is distinctive with minimal pairs (p.62); corroborates the lexical component; different dialect from Imyan.
